chapter.title: Forwarding Refs
chapter.description: Letting a parent reach the DOM node inside your component.

blocks.text: A ref placed on your own component does not reach the DOM, because `ref` is not a normal prop. `forwardRef` passes it through to the element you choose.

In React 19 `ref` became a normal prop for function components, so `forwardRef` is no longer required there. Plenty of codebases still run React 18, where it is, and libraries keep using it for compatibility.
Exposing a limited API with useImperativeHandle
Sometimes you want the parent to call specific methods rather than get the raw node. `useImperativeHandle` lets you decide what `ref.current` contains.
Keep the exposed surface small. A narrow imperative API is far easier to maintain than handing out the whole DOM node, and it stops callers depending on internals.

blocks.title: Build a small mutable box
blocks.instructions: Write createRef so it returns an object with a current property initialised to the given value, and so assigning to current works.

tests.name: It starts with the initial value
current can be reassigned
tests.code: var b = createRef(0); b.current = 3; return b.current === 3;

tests.name: Each call returns a separate box
tests.code: var a = createRef(1); var b = createRef(1); a.current = 9; return b.current === 1;

blocks.text: Pass a ref object to an element's `ref` attribute and React sets `current` to the DOM node after the commit.
`inputRef.current` is `null` during the first render, because the DOM node does not exist yet. Read it inside an effect or an event handler, never in the render body.
Refs are an escape hatch. Use them for things the declarative model genuinely cannot express.

items: Handing a node to a canvas or charting library.

blocks.text: Do not use a ref to set text, classes or styles by hand. React will overwrite your changes on the next render, and the two sources of truth will fight each other.
A ref can also be a function. React calls it with the node when it mounts and with `null` when it unmounts, which is useful when you need to react to the node appearing.

blocks.caption: One ref holding a Map is easier than trying to create refs in a loop.

blocks.text: Keeping a callback fresh without re-subscribing
When an effect should not re-run but needs the latest version of a callback, park the callback in a ref.

items: Reading `ref.current` during render. It may be `null`, and reading it makes the render impure.
Writing to a ref during render for the same reason - do it in an effect or a handler.
Using a ref for something the UI displays. That is state.
Using a ref to avoid a dependency warning. Fix the dependency instead.

blocks.text: Refs are deliberately an escape hatch. Every ref in a component is a small piece of imperative code inside a declarative system, so it is worth asking each time whether state or a key would do the job.
